title: Yielding
summary: Pausing the current thread without blocking the game: task.wait, WaitForChild, InvokeServer, Completed:Wait all yield. Other threads keep running; the yielded one resumes later. Know which calls yield — and avoid yielding in hot paths.

explanation.whatItIs: When code yields, its thread naps at that exact line and the engine schedules it to wake up later (after time passes, an event fires, a response returns). The rest of the game never notices.
explanation.whyItExists: Waiting is constant in games (delays, responses, loading). Yielding turns 'wait' from a freeze into a polite pause.
whenToUse: task.wait for delays; WaitForChild for replication; InvokeServer for answers
Event:Wait() inside spawned threads for sequencing
Designing APIs: document whether YOUR functions yield
whenNotToUse: In RenderStepped / hot loops — a yield there stalls your frame logic
Where you need the result RIGHT NOW on the same line for rendering math
explanation.mentalModel:
```text
Thread A:   print("a")
            task.wait(1)      ← A naps here
            print("b")        ← A wakes a second later

Meanwhile: other threads, physics, rendering — all continue.
Yielding ≠ freezing. It's thread-level cooperation.
```
tips: If a function might yield, call it in task.spawn when you can't afford the pause
Event:Wait() is powerful for one-shot sequencing — but pair with timeouts
Chains of yields are fine; deep yield stacks are usually a design smell
commonMistakes: Forgetting a function yields and writing frame-dependent code after it
Deadlocks: thread A waits for something only thread B can fire, while B waits for A

examples.title: Yield vs spawn
examples.code:
-- This WHOLE handler pauses at wait:
part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    task.wait(1)               -- handler thread naps 1s
    print("late:", hit.Name)
end)

-- Keep the handler snappy; offload the waiting:
part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    task.delay(1, function()
        print("delayed:", hit.Name)
    end)
end)
